query: For high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation? Specify what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, the expected observations relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy-alloy (HEA) multilayer protective coatings, resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation is governed primarily by interface-controlled kinetics: semi-coherent, chemically complex interfaces produce high barriers to both dislocation transmission/climb and vacancy diffusion. This raises the apparent activation energy for creep and shifts deformation from diffusion-controlled to interface-impeded dislocation-mediated creep, thereby lowering the steady-state creep rate compared with compositionally equivalent monolithic HEA films or simple (binary/ternary) multilayers at the same temperature and stress.
generation.material_initial_state: A sputtered monolithic HEA thin film coating (e.g., equiatomic multi-principal-element alloy) on a hard substrate, nanocrystalline with grain size ~50–200 nm, thickness ~1–2 µm, as-deposited, with minimal porosity and no intentional layering.
generation.intervention: Architectural nanolayering of the same average HEA chemistry into an HEA/HEA multilayer with 5–15 nm bilayer thickness engineered to form semi-coherent or low-angle semi-coherent interfaces (via pairing closely lattice-matched but compositionally distinct HEA sub-layers), followed by a low-temperature anneal (≤0.5 Tm) to promote interfacial short-range order without coarsening.
generation.conditions: Creep testing at 0.3–0.5 Tm of the average alloy (in Kelvin) in vacuum or inert gas under constant applied stress (e.g., micropillar compression at 200–800 MPa) or constant-load nanoindentation for 10^2–10^4 s; structural stability checks before/after testing to confirm layer integrity.
generation.structural_mediator: Semi-coherent, chemically complex interfaces exhibiting short-range order/segregation and modulus/chemical misfit, with a dense network of misfit dislocations that confines glide (confined layer slip) and impedes dislocation climb/transmission; concurrently, reduced effective interfacial diffusivity for vacancies/solute.
generation.mechanism: Interfaces act as rate-limiting barriers: (i) dislocation segments accumulate at interfaces and require higher activation work to transmit or climb, increasing the stress exponent; (ii) vacancy flux needed for climb and diffusional creep is slowed by chemically complex, compositionally disordered interfacial regions ("sluggish" interfacial diffusion), increasing the apparent activation energy. As a result, the multilayer transitions creep toward an interface-impeded dislocation mechanism with lower steady-state creep rates than the monolithic HEA or simple multilayers at matched conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the monolithic HEA baseline at the same temperature and stress: (a) steady-state creep rate reduced by a factor of roughly 5–20 in the multilayer when bilayer thickness is ≤15 nm; (b) higher apparent activation energy for creep by approximately 30–60%; (c) higher stress exponent n indicative of reduced diffusion control; (d) nanoindentation dwell depth increases 30–70% less over 10^3 s; (e) in-situ TEM shows dislocation pile-ups and infrequent transmission at interfaces; (f) tracer/SIMS measurements indicate ≥2–5× lower effective interfacial diffusivity. Magnitudes are approximate and may vary with chemistry and interface coherency.
generation.baseline: A monolithic HEA film of the same average composition, thickness, and grain size deposited under identical conditions; optionally, a simple binary/ternary metallic multilayer with similar bilayer thickness and average modulus as an additional control.
generation.boundary: Effect is expected when: (i) bilayer thickness ≤20 nm so deformation is interface-dominated; (ii) interfaces remain semi-coherent and chemically complex without gross intermixing; (iii) grains are at least comparable to or larger than bilayer thickness to maintain layer continuity; (iv) testing temperature ≤0.5–0.6 Tm and environment is inert (oxidation absent). The effect diminishes if layers coarsen, interfaces lose coherency/SRO, substantial amorphization occurs, grain-boundary sliding dominates at higher homologous temperatures, or residual stress/texture artifacts dominate deformation.
generation.uncertainty: No direct supporting evidence is provided here; the magnitude of rate reduction and changes in activation parameters are uncertain and chemistry-dependent. The extent and stability of interfacial short-range order/segregation in specific HEA pairs are uncertain, and residual stresses, texture, or grain size differences could confound comparisons. Some HEA systems may not exhibit significantly reduced interfacial diffusivity.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three coatings on identical substrates: (1) monolithic HEA film (baseline); (2) HEA/HEA multilayer with 5–10 nm bilayers engineered for semi-coherent interfaces; (3) simple binary/ternary multilayer with similar bilayer thickness and average modulus contrast. Verify microstructures (STEM-HAADF, GPA for coherency, APT/EDS for interfacial chemistry, XRD for layer periodicity). Conduct constant-stress micropillar creep (multiple stresses, 0.3–0.5 Tm) and constant-load nanoindentation dwell tests (10^2–10^4 s). Determine steady-state creep rate, stress exponent n, and activation energy Q via temperature-stress mapping. Perform in-situ TEM straining to quantify dislocation-interface transmission/climb events and radiotracer or SIMS to estimate effective interfacial diffusivity. Optionally anneal a subset to disrupt interfacial SRO (mild intermixing) and repeat tests.
measurements: Steady-state creep rate vs. stress and temperature
Apparent activation energy Q for creep
Nanoindentation dwell depth vs. time at fixed load
Dislocation-interface transmission/climb frequency from in-situ TEM
Bilayer thickness and coherency before/after testing (STEM/XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if, after confirming comparable grain size and layer integrity, the HEA multilayer does not exhibit at least a statistically significant (>2×) reduction in steady-state creep rate relative to the monolithic HEA at matched stress/temperature, and does not show increased Q or n, nor reduced interfacial diffusivity or observable dislocation blocking at interfaces. Additionally, if intentional disruption of interfacial chemical order/coherency does not measurably degrade creep resistance, the mechanism as stated is falsified.
